title: An in-game camera the engine actually judges — framing, fill, focus and facing, scored per shot
excerpt: A screenshot plugin writes a PNG to the hard drive and nothing in the game knows it happened. This one develops a print the events can read back — and sixty photographs cost about 55 KB of save file.
body: Screenshot plugins already exist and they are free. This is not one of those. A screenshot writes a PNG to the player’s hard drive; nothing inside the game ever knows it happened, so nothing in the game can ever ask for one. Aperture Core gives the player a lens instead. They frame a shot, rack focus, choose an aperture and press the shutter — and the engine judges the photograph. Six things are scored: framing, how near the subject sits to the frame centre or one of the four rule-of-thirds intersections, so a deliberate off-centre composition scores as well as a centred one; fill, how much of the frame the subject occupies, which is why a speck on the horizon and a cropped nose both score badly; focus, against a depth of field derived from the chosen aperture and focal length, so wide open at f1.8 you have centimetres and at f11 almost everything is sharp; facing, because a creature looking at the lens is a better photograph than the back of its head; company, a group bonus that stops paying once the shot is clutter; and balance, where the mass of the shot sits in the frame. Making something photographable is one notetag in the note box of any event, actor or enemy — the subject’s key and display name, optionally with its height in tiles, a rarity from 1 to 5 and the base value of a perfect shot. That is the entire authoring burden. There is no separate database, no per-map registry and no setup event. Photo requests turn that into quests. A request is a commission — photograph this subject, at least this well — and the moment a qualifying print lands in the album the request completes, readable from a plugin command or a script call. The part worth reading before you install anything is why your save file does not explode. A photograph is not stored as an image. Each print keeps a small indexed-colour thumbnail — 48×36 in 16 colours, about 900 bytes — plus the shot’s descriptor: where the camera was, what was in frame, and how it scored. Sixty photographs cost roughly 55 KB. A single PNG data URI would have cost more than that on its own, and there would have been sixty of them. The print you see in the album is re-developed from that descriptor every time it is displayed, which is also why prints look like prints rather than like screenshots. Where to get it: the itch.io page linked above. It is a “name your own price” listing — you can set your own amount, including zero, so you can try it before deciding what it is worth to you. The download ships readable, unobfuscated JavaScript — no minification — plus a LICENSE.txt. Commercial use in your games is permitted; redistribution of the plugin source itself is not, which is why this entry links to the plugin rather than hosting the file. AI disclosure: the code and the store images for this plugin were generated with AI assistance, and this is disclosed on the itch.io listing as well. Note on the help text below: this site cannot display angle-bracket characters — it deletes anything that looks like a tag, which would silently remove the notetags below. Aperture Core’s help uses 4 angle brackets, written here as ⟨ and ⟩. Nothing else has been changed: every other character is exactly as it ships inside the plugin. When you copy a notetag into your own project, type the ordinary < and > characters.
help:
============================================================================
Aperture Core — the camera your player actually aims
============================================================================

Screenshot plugins already exist and they are free. This is not one. A
screenshot plugin writes a PNG to the player's hard drive; nothing in the
game ever knows it happened.

Aperture Core gives the player a lens. They frame a shot, rack focus, choose
an aperture, and press the shutter — and the ENGINE judges the photograph:
what is in it, how well it is composed, whether the subject is sharp, and
whether it was worth taking. The result is a developed print that lands in an
album, satisfies photo requests, and can be read back by your events.

WHAT THE ENGINE SCORES
----------------------
  framing    how near the subject sits to a power point — the frame centre
             or one of the four rule-of-thirds intersections. Deliberate
             off-centre composition scores as well as a centred one, which
             is the whole reason the rule exists.
  fill       how much of the frame the subject occupies. A speck on the
             horizon and a cropped nose both score badly.
  focus      how near the subject is to the focal plane, against a depth of
             field derived from the chosen aperture and focal length. Wide
             open at f1.8 you have centimetres; at f11 almost everything is
             sharp.
  facing     a creature looking at the lens is a better photograph than the
             back of its head.
  company    extra subjects in frame earn a group bonus, until there are so
             many that the shot is clutter.
  balance    where the mass of the shot sits relative to the frame.

MAKING SOMETHING PHOTOGRAPHABLE
-------------------------------
Put a notetag in the note box of any event, actor or enemy:

    ⟨photo: forest_wolf, Grey Wolf⟩
    ⟨photo: forest_wolf, Grey Wolf, size=1.6, rarity=3, points=180⟩

  size     how tall the subject is in tiles. Decides how much frame it
           fills at a given distance. 1.0 is a person; 3.0 is a bear.
  rarity   1..5. Multiplies the shot's value and sorts the album.
  points   the base value of a perfect photograph of this subject.

That is the entire authoring burden. There is no separate database, no
per-map registry and no setup event.

PHOTO REQUESTS
--------------
A request is a commission: photograph this subject, at least this well.

    ApertureCore.addRequest('wolf_job', 'forest_wolf', 'B',
                            'The innkeeper wants proof of the wolf.')

The moment a qualifying print lands in the album the request completes, and
your events can read it back with the plugin command "Check request" or with
ApertureCore.isRequestDone(id).

WHY YOUR SAVE FILE DOES NOT EXPLODE
-----------------------------------
This is the trap every in-game camera falls into, so it was designed out
first. A photograph is NOT stored as an image. Each print keeps a small
indexed-colour thumbnail — 48x36 in 16 colours is about 900 bytes — plus the
shot's descriptor: where the camera was, what was in frame, how it scored.
Sixty photographs cost roughly 55 KB. A single PNG data URI would have cost
more than that on its own, and there would have been sixty of them.

The print you see in the album is re-developed from that data every time it
is displayed. That is also why prints look like prints and not like
screenshots.

PLUGIN COMMANDS
---------------
  Open camera      hands the player the viewfinder
  Open album       opens the developed album
  Add request      commissions a photograph
  Check request    writes 1 or 0 into a switch
  Give camera      gates the camera behind an item, if you want it gated

COMPATIBILITY
-------------
Every core method this touches is patched by prototype extension with the
original saved and called. Nothing is overwritten. It does not replace the
map scene, the menu, or any window class your other plugins may also touch.
